title: The Detention Paradox
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau takes on the commonplace claim that detentions "don't work" because the pupils who collect the most of them keep misbehaving. He argues that this judges the sanction by its least representative recipients, much like evaluating speed cameras by interviewing only drivers who were caught speeding. Drawing on Atkins et al., Fluke et al. and experimental work on third-party punishment, he shows that sanctions seem to change behaviour for many students while failing for a persistent, highly aggressive minority. He adds the "spreading of disorder" field experiments, in which visible unpunished rule-breaking made other people more likely to break unrelated rules. His conclusion is that detentions mainly work for the majority who go with the flow, because each enforced rule tells the whole community what the norms are. Certainty, proportionality and fairness matter more than severity, and a pupil on their fiftieth detention needs something else without that making the first 49 pointless.
points: Evaluating detention by the students who keep receiving it is a selection error, since the most persistent offenders are by definition unrepresentative of how sanctions affect everyone else.

In the Atkins et al. study, students who responded to detention ended up statistically equivalent to unsanctioned peers, while the group that kept accumulating referrals were rated highly aggressive and low in social skills.
Sanctions communicate social norms to observers: seeing a rule enforced tells everyone watching that "that's not what we do round here".
Keizer and colleagues' graffiti experiments show disorder spreads, so unsanctioned violations lower compliance with unrelated rules across the whole school.

Certainty, proportionality and fairness matter more than severity, and a school should find something different for the student with the fiftieth detention rather than abandon the sanction for the other 49.
quotes: The problem wasn’t that sanctions didn’t work but that they only appeared to work for some students.

But using the behaviour of this group to judge whether detention deters students in general is like evaluating the effectiveness of speed cameras by only interviewing drivers who’ve been caught speeding. The most persistent offenders are, by definition, unrepresentative.
Experimental research on ‘third-party punishment’ has found that when people see someone punished for violating a norm, it changes their beliefs about what others approve of.

Keizer and colleagues called this the ‘spreading of disorder’ — a phenomenon all too common in schools. Observing violations, particularly those that go unsanctioned, reduces the likelihood of rules being followed in general.

There’s little reason to think that making a detention two hours long rather than one will somehow transform behaviour. Excessive or arbitrary punishment undermines the legitimacy on which effective discipline depends.
A rule which is repeatedly broken without consequence stops functioning as a rule. Students quickly learn what will be tolerated and adjust the behaviour accordingly.

So, here’s my conclusion: detentions only work for those kids who go with the flow. It would be obviously wrong to punish children who always behave well and kids who, like my younger self, always seem to do the wrong thing are unlikely to be persuaded by consequences they routinely fail to see coming.
